title: Find pairs of employees who have the same salary (across the whole list).
shortTitle: Find pairs of employees who have the same salary
keyPoints: groupingBy(getSalary) groups employees by salary amount into Map<BigDecimal, List<Employee>>
Filter groups with size > 1 to find salary values shared by multiple employees
For actual pairs, generate combinations from each group using nested iteration: N*(N-1)/2 pairs
BigDecimal.compareTo == 0 checks value equality, while equals also checks scale (1000000 != 1000000.00)
Ensure consistent BigDecimal scale before grouping so equals-based groupingBy works correctly
The groupBy approach is O(n) whereas comparing all pairs with nested loops is O(n^2)

s1_definition.oneliner: Group employees by salary with `groupingBy(getSalary)`, then filter groups with more than one employee to find same-salary pairs.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **groupingBy(getSalary)** produces `Map<BigDecimal, List<Employee>>` bucketed by salary amount.
- **Filter size > 1** keeps salary groups where multiple employees earn the same amount.
- **Pair generation** from each group of N employees produces N*(N-1)/2 unique pairs via nested iteration.
- **BigDecimal equality** matters: `equals` checks both value and scale, so ensure consistent scale before grouping.
- **O(n) grouping** is far more efficient than O(n^2) all-pairs comparison.
s1_definition.analogy: The payroll auditor at National Bank of India suspects some employees were given identical salaries by mistake. She groups all pay slips by the salary amount on each slip and flags any pile with more than one slip for review.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Input: [Rajesh 1.8M, Priya 1M, Kavita 1M, Deepak 1.5M, Ananya 0.9M, Suresh 0.9M]
       │
       │  groupingBy(salary)
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Rs.1800K → [Rajesh]             (1) ✗  │
  │  Rs.1500K → [Deepak]             (1) ✗  │
  │  Rs.1000K → [Priya, Kavita]      (2) ✓  │
  │  Rs.900K  → [Ananya, Suresh]     (2) ✓  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
       │
       │  filter(size > 1)  →  generate pairs
       ▼
  Pairs: (Priya, Kavita), (Ananya, Suresh)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding same-salary pairs groups employees by salary amount using `groupingBy` and then filters for groups with more than one member. Within each matching group, nested iteration with the inner loop starting at `i + 1` generates unique pairs without duplicates.

At the National Bank of India, the payroll auditor uses this pattern to flag employees who may have been assigned identical salaries by mistake. The groupBy approach is O(n) for grouping, far more efficient than comparing all possible pairs in O(n^2). The per-group pair generation is O(k^2) where k is the group size, but k is typically small.

The critical subtlety is `BigDecimal.equals` versus `compareTo`. The `equals` method checks both value and scale, so `1000000` and `1000000.00` are not equal by `equals` but are equal by `compareTo`. Since `groupingBy` uses `equals` internally, you must normalize the scale of salary values before grouping, or the same pay amount could end up in separate buckets.

Remember one sentence: `groupBy(salary)` then `filter(size > 1)` finds employees earning the same amount, and nested iteration within each group generates the actual pairs.
